# Render3D Profile 1: the numbers and the rules

Specification hash: `8888f0994b3a6bb725f14df420833c2aa64992eb9679c4ae8971a2c00b2d6a84`

`Render3D Core Profile 1`'s feature list says what a backend must be able to do. This document says
what the answers are. Two backends can implement every feature in that list and produce different
images; every difference they could produce is a question answered here.

## Conventions

| convention | value |
| --- | --- |
| clip volume | `-w <= x <= w, -w <= y <= w, 0 <= z <= w, with w > 0 for a visible point` |
| clip plane order | w = CLIP_W_EPSILON, then z >= 0, then z <= w, then x >= -w, then x <= w, then y >= -w, then y <= w |
| horizon epsilon | 0.00000095367431640625 (the same value the 2D profile uses) |
| NDC y direction | down, matching the 2D device space and the scanout's row order |
| front face | counter-clockwise in NDC |
| pixel centres | half-integers, as in the 2D profile |

## `ClipCoordQ`

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| what it is | four `f32` components x, y, z, w in the clip volume above, produced by the vertex stage and consumed by the clipper before any divide |
| the arithmetic it is clipped in | HOMOGENEOUS and at `f32`, before the perspective divide. Dividing first and clipping after produces coordinates of ten million pixels for a vertex just behind the eye, and a rasteriser that spends a frame on one triangle |
| a non-finite component | the PRIMITIVE is refused, not the vertex. A NaN or an infinity in any component makes every inequality above false, so a clipper cannot decide the primitive at all - and silently dropping it would make a shader bug look like a culling rule |
| w <= 0 on every vertex | the primitive is entirely behind the eye and is dropped. This is a CULL and not a refusal: it is the ordinary state of geometry behind the camera |
| w <= 0 on some vertices | the primitive is clipped against the `w = CLIP_W_EPSILON` plane FIRST, and the remaining planes afterwards. Clipping against `w = 0` exactly produces a vertex at infinity after the divide |
| the epsilon | `CLIP_W_EPSILON`, and it is a value rather than an implementation's guess |
| whether a backend may clip in a different space | NO. A backend that clips after the divide, or in fixed point, produces different vertices at the same input, and the conformance suite compares vertices |

## Interpolation qualifiers, and what clipping does to them

| qualifier | across the primitive | at a clip intersection | why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `smooth` | perspective-correct: the value is interpolated as `v/w` against `1/w` and divided back at the sample, so the result is the value at the point the sample corresponds to on the surface | HOMOGENEOUS edge interpolation. For endpoints P0 and P1 cut at parameter `t` computed from the homogeneous plane equation, every component INCLUDING `w` is interpolated linearly at that `t`, and the attribute follows the same `t` | the `t` that makes the position correct is the `t` that makes a perspective-correct attribute correct, because both are linear in homogeneous space |
| `noperspective` | linear in SCREEN space: the value is interpolated against the barycentric coordinates of the projected triangle, with no `1/w` weighting | PROJECTED edge interpolation. The parameter is recomputed from the PROJECTED endpoints - `t_screen` - and the attribute follows that, not the homogeneous `t` | an attribute declared to be linear on the screen must stay linear on the screen after a cut; using the homogeneous `t` would put a kink at the clip edge, which is visible as a bent line in exactly the wrong place |
| `flat` | constant, taken from the PROVOKING vertex of the primitive as assembled, before any clipping | UNCHANGED. The value of the ORIGINAL primitive's provoking vertex is carried onto every fragment, INCLUDING when that vertex was clipped away entirely | a flat attribute identifies the primitive - a material index, an object id - and a clipped triangle is the same triangle. Taking the value from a vertex the clipper invented would make an id depend on where the camera is |
| `centroid` | as its base qualifier, evaluated at a point INSIDE the covered part of the pixel rather than at the pixel centre | as its base qualifier. `centroid` chooses an evaluation LOCATION and does not change the interpolation rule | at an edge the pixel centre can lie outside the primitive, and extrapolating a texture coordinate there samples outside the surface - which is the shimmer along silhouettes that multisampling is supposed to remove |
| `sample` | as its base qualifier, evaluated once per COVERED SAMPLE rather than once per pixel | as its base qualifier, for the same reason as `centroid` | it is what makes per-sample shading mean anything: a fragment shader run once per pixel cannot produce different values at two samples of it |

Rounding: the intersection parameter and every interpolated attribute are computed at `f32` and kept at `f32`; no backend may compute them at a wider precision and round, because the conformance suite compares positions bit-exactly under StrictF32

### The provoking vertex

| topology | which vertex |
| --- | --- |
| triangle list | the FIRST vertex of each triangle: 3i |
| triangle strip | the FIRST vertex of each triangle in emission order: vertex i of the strip for triangle i, whatever the winding flip does to the other two |
| triangle fan | the SECOND vertex of each triangle - the one that is not the shared hub. The hub is in every triangle, so choosing it would give every triangle of a fan the same flat value |
| line list | the FIRST vertex of each line: 2i |
| line strip | the FIRST vertex of each segment: vertex i for segment i |
| point list | the point itself |
| after fan triangulation | a clipped polygon is triangulated as a FAN from its first vertex, and every resulting triangle carries the ORIGINAL primitive's provoking value - the triangulation is an implementation detail of clipping and must not be visible in a flat attribute |
| after primitive restart | the strip or fan begins again, so the next primitive's provoking vertex is the first of the NEW run |

## Colour formats

| format | full name | bits | sampled | filterable | renderable | blendable | MSAA | vertex | readback | attachment |
| --- | --- | ---: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| `R8` | R8_UNORM: one 8-bit channel, unsigned normalised to [0, 1] | 8 | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | yes | yes |
| `RG8` | R8G8_UNORM: two 8-bit channels, unsigned normalised to [0, 1] | 16 | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | yes | yes |
| `RGBA8` | R8G8B8A8_UNORM: four 8-bit channels, unsigned normalised to [0, 1], NOT sRGB-encoded | 32 | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | yes | yes |
| `RGB10A2` | A2B10G10R10_UNORM_PACK32: three 10-bit channels and two bits of alpha, unsigned normalised | 32 | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | yes | yes |
| `RGBA16F` | R16G16B16A16_SFLOAT: four IEEE 754 binary16 channels | 64 | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no | yes | yes |
| `RGBA32F` | R32G32B32A32_SFLOAT: four IEEE 754 binary32 channels | 128 | yes | no | yes | no | no | no | yes | yes |
| `R32Uint` | R32_UINT: one 32-bit unsigned integer channel, not normalised | 32 | yes | no | yes | no | yes | no | yes | yes |

- **RGBA32F is not filterable**: a 128-bit filtered fetch is four 32-bit lerps per tap and eight taps for trilinear, which is a cost no software backend can meet at a frame rate and no hardware backend guarantees. `MinNearest`/`MagNearest` are the conforming way to sample it
- **RGBA32F is not blendable and not multisampled**: for the same reason: a blend is a read-modify-write of 128 bits per sample, and multisampling multiplies it. A pass that needs full float precision needs one sample and no blending, and saying so is better than a backend discovering it
- **an integer format is not filterable or blendable**: there is no correct answer to what the average of two object ids is, and blending them produces an id that identifies nothing. It IS multisampled, because coverage still applies - the resolve rule for it is stated with the MSAA rules

## Vertex formats

| format | full name | bytes | shader type |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| `Float32` | R32_SFLOAT | 4 | `f32` |
| `Float32x2` | R32G32_SFLOAT | 8 | `vec2` |
| `Float32x3` | R32G32B32_SFLOAT | 12 | `vec3` |
| `Float32x4` | R32G32B32A32_SFLOAT | 16 | `vec4` |
| `Unorm8x4` | R8G8B8A8_UNORM | 4 | `vec4 in [0, 1]` |
| `Snorm8x4` | R8G8B8A8_SNORM | 4 | `vec4 in [-1, 1]` |
| `Unorm16x2` | R16G16_UNORM | 4 | `vec2 in [0, 1]` |
| `Unorm16x4` | R16G16B16A16_UNORM | 8 | `vec4 in [0, 1]` |
| `Uint16x2` | R16G16_UINT | 4 | `uvec2` |
| `Uint32` | R32_UINT | 4 | `u32` |

- **unsigned normalised**: `value / MAX`, so an 8-bit 255 is exactly 1.0 and 0 is exactly 0.0
- **signed normalised**: `max(value / MAX_POSITIVE, -1.0)`, so an 8-bit 127 is exactly 1.0, -127 is exactly -1.0, and -128 CLAMPS to -1.0 rather than producing -1.0079. The other convention - dividing by 128 - makes 127 fall short of 1.0, which shows up as a normal that is not unit length
- **alignment**: an attribute's offset within its stream must be a multiple of the size of its largest component; an unaligned layout is REFUSED at pipeline creation rather than working on one backend

## Rasteriser state

| state | values | default | why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fill mode | solid | `solid` | wireframe is a DIFFERENT primitive topology in this profile, not a rasteriser mode: a line-list draw produces lines a backend can define exactly, where wireframe fill leaves every implementation to invent its own edge rule |
| cull mode | none | front | back | `back` | back by default because the commonest mistake is forgetting to set it and seeing interior faces, which is a wrong picture rather than a slow one |
| front face | counter-clockwise | clockwise | `counter-clockwise` | counter-clockwise in NDC, and NDC has y down - so what a reader sees on the screen as counter-clockwise is front-facing |
| depth clamp | off | `off` | clamping instead of clipping at the near plane changes what a depth value means, and a profile that offered both would have two depth semantics |
| depth bias | constant factor, slope factor, clamp; each an f32 | `0, 0, 0` | shadow-map acne is not solvable without it, and the exact equation is stated below rather than left to a backend |
| line width | 1.0 | `1.0` | a fixed width of one pixel. Wide lines are ten different rasterisation rules across implementations, and the 2D profile is where a stroked line with a defined join belongs |
| scissor | one rectangle in pixels, clamped to the attachment | `the whole attachment` | one and not an array: a per-viewport scissor array needs a viewport array, which this profile does not have |
| viewport | x, y, width, height, min depth, max depth | `the whole attachment, depth 0 to 1` | the depth range is part of the viewport because that is where NDC z becomes a depth value, and stating it anywhere else splits one transform in two |

Depth bias: offset = constant_factor * r + slope_factor * m, where m is the maximum of |dz/dx| and |dz/dy| over the primitive and r is the smallest representable difference at the depth format's precision near the fragment's depth; for a floating-point depth format r is 2^(exponent(z) - 23). The offset is added AFTER the depth value is computed and BEFORE the depth test and the depth write. A non-zero clamp bounds |offset|

## Multisampling

Positions are in the pixel's own [0, 1] space with the origin at its top-left corner.

| count | sample | x | y |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2x | 0 | 0.75 | 0.75 |
| 2x | 1 | 0.25 | 0.25 |
| 4x | 0 | 0.375 | 0.125 |
| 4x | 1 | 0.875 | 0.375 |
| 4x | 2 | 0.125 | 0.625 |
| 4x | 3 | 0.625 | 0.875 |

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| shading frequency | ONCE PER PIXEL by default, with the result written to every covered sample. Per-sample shading happens only where an input is declared `sample`, and then the fragment stage runs once per covered sample |
| the centroid rule | a `centroid` input is evaluated at the CENTRE OF MASS of the covered sample positions. Where no sample is covered - which cannot happen for a fragment that exists - it is the pixel centre. It is NOT a covered sample's position: an average is stable as coverage changes, where 'the first covered sample' jumps between pixels along an edge |
| sample mask order | bit i of a sample mask is sample i as indexed above, least significant bit first. A mask is ANDed with coverage BEFORE the depth test, so a masked-out sample is not tested and not written |
| alpha to coverage | coverage is ANDed with the first `round(alpha * sample_count)` sample bits IN INDEX ORDER, where alpha is attachment 0's alpha after the fragment stage and before blending. In index order rather than by a dither pattern, because a pattern makes the result depend on the pixel's position and two adjacent pixels with the same alpha get different coverage |
| colour resolve | the ARITHMETIC MEAN of the samples, computed in the attachment's own numeric space and rounded once at the end. Averaging in a different space - sRGB-encoded values, say - is the classic resolve that darkens edges |
| integer resolve | sample 0 is taken and the rest are discarded. There is no average of two object ids that identifies anything, and a resolve that produced one would invent an id |
| depth resolve | sample 0 is taken. A depth buffer's resolved value is used for reconstruction, and the MINIMUM of the samples belongs to whichever surface is nearest rather than to the surface the colour resolve is mostly made of |
| stencil resolve | sample 0 is taken, for the same reason as the integer case |
| a resolve to a different format | REFUSED. A resolve is an average and not a conversion; a pass that wants both states both |

## Depth and stencil

| format | full name | storage | stored range | comparison |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Depth16` | D16_UNORM | 16-bit unsigned normalised | [0, 1] mapped to [0, 65535] | the stored integers are compared |
| `Depth24` | X8_D24_UNORM_PACK32 | 24-bit unsigned normalised in the low bits of a 32-bit word | [0, 1] mapped to [0, 16777215] | the stored integers are compared |
| `Depth32F` | D32_SFLOAT | IEEE 754 binary32 | [0, 1] as floating point, with the whole mantissa spent near 0 | THE STORED FLOATS ARE COMPARED - see `DEPTH32F_ANSWER` |
| `Depth24Stencil8` | D24_UNORM_S8_UINT | 24-bit unsigned normalised depth and an 8-bit unsigned stencil | depth [0, 1] mapped to [0, 16777215]; stencil [0, 255] | the stored integers are compared |
| `Depth32FStencil8` | D32_SFLOAT_S8_UINT | IEEE 754 binary32 depth and an 8-bit unsigned stencil, separately addressed | depth [0, 1] as floating point; stencil [0, 255] | the stored floats are compared |

### The `Depth32F` question

THE STORED FLOATS ARE COMPARED, AND THE INCOMING DEPTH IS NOT QUANTISED. A fragment's depth is computed at f32, clamped to the viewport's depth range, and compared against the stored f32 exactly. Quantisation is what a normalised format does because its storage cannot hold anything else; imposing it on a float format would throw away the precision the format exists for. The consequence is stated so nobody has to discover it: a second pass over the same geometry must use `LessOrEqual` AND must compute depth by the same path, which under this profile's StrictF32 rules it does - the vertex stage is bit-exact, so the same vertices produce the same depth

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| the compare operations | Never, Less, Equal, LessOrEqual, Greater, NotEqual, GreaterOrEqual, Always - applied as `incoming OP stored` |
| when the depth write happens | after the depth test passes and after the stencil test passes, and never when either fails. A fragment discarded by the fragment stage writes neither |
| clamping | the incoming depth is clamped to the viewport's [min depth, max depth] AFTER the bias and BEFORE the test, so a bias cannot push a fragment outside the buffer's range |
| clear | a depth clear takes an f32 in [0, 1] and is converted to the format's storage by the same rule a fragment's depth is; a stencil clear takes a u32 and its low 8 bits are stored |
| stencil test order | stencil test first, then depth test. The stencil op selected depends on BOTH: `fail` when the stencil test fails, `depth-fail` when the stencil passed and the depth failed, `pass` when both passed |
| readback | a depth readback answers the STORED values converted to f32 in [0, 1], not the raw integers, so a caller does not have to know the storage |

## Sampling

LOD: lambda = log2(rho) + bias, clamped to [min_lod, max_lod] and then to [0, level_count - 1], where rho is the MAXIMUM of the lengths of the two texture-coordinate derivative vectors in texels: rho = max(length(ddx(uv) * size), length(ddy(uv) * size)). The maximum rather than a geometric mean, because the mean under-filters exactly where an anisotropic footprint is worst

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| tap count, nearest | one tap at the texel whose centre is nearest the sample point; a tie goes to the LOWER index in each dimension, so the rule is total and two backends round the same way |
| tap count, linear within a level | four taps in 2D, eight in 3D, weighted by the fractional position of the sample point relative to texel CENTRES, computed at f32 |
| tap count, trilinear | two levels linearly filtered and blended by frac(lambda), which is eight taps in 2D. When lambda is at or above the last level, the last level alone is used and no blend happens |
| the footprint | the derivatives of the texture coordinate with respect to the FRAGMENT's x and y in the attachment's pixel space, evaluated at the sample location. In a fragment stage they come from a 2x2 quad; where no quad exists - a vertex-stage fetch - the explicit-LOD form is the only legal one |
| anisotropic sampling | up to 8 taps along the major axis of the footprint, each a full filtered sample at the level chosen from the MINOR axis, averaged with equal weights. The tap count is `min(ceil(major/minor), max_anisotropy)`; with max_anisotropy 1 the rule collapses to the isotropic one above |
| cube-face orientation | the six faces are +X, -X, +Y, -Y, +Z, -Z in that index order, with the same major-axis selection and the same s/t sign conventions the standard cube-map table defines - so a cube built for any other system loads without a flip |
| the cube seam rule | a linear filter whose footprint crosses a face edge TAKES THE TAPS FROM THE NEIGHBOURING FACE, not from a clamped edge texel. Clamping is what makes the seam visible, and a profile that left it open would make every cube map look different on two backends |
| the mip-generation kernel | a 2x2 BOX filter of the level above, averaged in the texture's own numeric space - linear for a float format, and for a normalised format the four integers are summed and divided with round-half-up. An odd dimension halves by `max(1, floor(n/2))` and the box takes the three or two texels that exist; there is no weighting to invent |
| depth-compare sampling | each tap is compared against the reference FIRST, producing 0.0 or 1.0, and the taps are then filtered - so a linear depth-compare sample is the FRACTION of taps that passed, which is what makes percentage-closer filtering work. Filtering the depths and comparing once produces a hard edge and is the wrong answer |
| the border colour | one of three values and not an arbitrary colour: transparent black (0,0,0,0), opaque black (0,0,0,1), opaque white (1,1,1,1). An arbitrary border needs a whole colour to travel with the sampler, and the three above cover every use a border wrap has |
| wrap modes | clamp-to-edge, repeat, mirrored-repeat and clamp-to-border, applied per axis before the texel fetch and AFTER the LOD is chosen - so a wrapped coordinate does not change the derivative the level came from |
| unnormalised coordinates | NOT IN THIS PROFILE. Every sample takes normalised coordinates; a fetch by integer texel is a different operation with its own rules and no filtering |

## Resource hazards

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| who is responsible | THE IMPLEMENTATION. A submitted command list observes every write made by every command list submitted before it, and every write made earlier within itself. An application never inserts a barrier, because a profile that required one would need to enumerate every barrier kind and every implementation would need the same ones |
| a texture read while it is an attachment | REFUSED at submission. The read has no defined value - it depends on tile order - and refusing it is the only answer that does not make the picture depend on the backend |
| a buffer written by the host while it is in flight | REFUSED: a resource handed to a submission is owned by that submission until its completion is observable. The refusal is at the WRITE, not at the submission, so the report names the thing that is wrong |
| read-after-write across passes | ordered by submission order. The result of a pass that writes a texture is visible to every later pass that samples it, with no action by the caller |
| write-after-read within one pass | REFUSED for the same reason as the attachment case: within a pass there is no order between fragments |
| two passes writing one attachment | ordered by submission order, and the load operation of the second decides what the first's output is worth - `Load` keeps it, `Clear` discards it, `Discard` says nobody may read it |
| whether the ordering costs a flush | that is the implementation's business. What the profile fixes is the OBSERVABLE order; a backend that can prove two passes do not touch the same memory may run them in either order |

## Submission and readback

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| what a submission is | one command list, submitted whole. A partially submitted list is not a state this profile has |
| ordering | submissions complete in the order they were submitted. A backend may execute them out of order only where nothing can observe it |
| how completion is observed | by a typed completion the submission answers with, not by a sleep and not by a query loop. The 2D profile's presentation completion has the same shape for the same reason |
| readback | a readback is a command IN a list and completes with it. A readback issued outside a list would need its own ordering rules against the lists around it |
| what a readback of an untouched attachment answers | the clear value where the pass cleared, and a REFUSAL where the pass discarded. Reading discarded content is how one backend's uninitialised memory becomes another's black |
| object-id readback | an integer attachment read back at a pixel, with the integer resolve rule above. It is in the profile because picking is not optional in an application, and every implementation that leaves it out grows a worse version of it |

## Guaranteed minimum limits

An implementation-defined limit without a floor lets a backend pass every other rule in this
document while being useless. The conformance suite runs against these minima rather than against
whatever a backend happens to offer.

| limit | minimum | why |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `max_texture_extent_2d` | 4096 | a 4K colour attachment is the size of one screen, and a backend that cannot hold one cannot render a frame |
| `max_texture_extent_3d` | 256 | a 256-cubed volume is the smallest useful one and fits in 64 MB at RGBA8 |
| `max_texture_layers` | 256 | one layer per shadow cascade, per material atlas page and per instance set |
| `max_colour_attachments` | 4 | a deferred pass needs colour, normal, material and an object id, which is four |
| `max_vertex_streams` | 4 | position, normal, texture coordinates and one instance stream |
| `max_vertex_attributes` | 16 | four streams of four attributes |
| `max_draws_per_pass` | 65536 | a scene of a few thousand objects with a few materials each, which is an ordinary scene and not a stress test |
| `max_shader_instructions` | 4096 | enough for a physically based material with four lights, which is the standard material this profile's scene layer ships |
| `max_uniform_bytes_per_stage` | 16384 | a 4x4 matrix per bone for 64 bones, plus the per-frame block |
| `max_samplers_per_stage` | 16 | a PBR material is five textures, and a pass has a shadow map and an environment map on top |
| `max_anisotropy` | 8 | the value the feature list names; below it the anisotropic rule above collapses to something the profile already has |

## Conformance thresholds

A suite without stated tolerances either demands bit-exactness, which no two implementations of a
sine achieve, or demands nothing. Both are ways of not checking. No tolerance may be loosened per
architecture.

| what is compared | tolerance | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a clip-space position | NONE. Bit-exact under StrictF32 | it is what makes two backends place a triangle in the same place, and a tolerance here is a tolerance on WHERE a picture is |
| sample ownership | NONE. A sample is covered or it is not, and the two backends must agree on every sample | coverage is decided by the frozen sample positions, so there is nothing left to round |
| an interpolated attribute | <= 4 ULP of f32 against the barycentric expression evaluated at f64 | the interpolation is three multiplies and two adds whose order the profile does not fix, which is worth a few ULP and nothing more |
| a depth value | <= 1 ULP for a floating-point format and EXACT for a normalised one | a normalised depth is an integer after the conversion, and an integer that differs is a different depth test |
| a filtered texture sample | <= 2/255 per channel for a normalised format and <= 1e-4 relative for a floating-point one | the taps and their weights are fixed by the sampler contract, so the remaining error is the weight arithmetic |
| a transcendental in a shader | the ULP bound `Shader IR 1` states for that operation, and no other | restating it here would be a second number to keep in step with the first |

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| per-architecture loosening | REFUSED. A tolerance that widened on the slow target would be a suite that stopped checking exactly where the second implementation is, which is the only place a comparison is worth making |
| what has no tolerance at all | clip-space positions, sample ownership, bit-exact classifications, normalised depth values and pick ids. Each is either an integer or is bit-exact by the StrictF32 rules, and a tolerance on one would be a tolerance on identity |
| where a tolerance is compared | in the NAMED comparison space - linear Rec. 709 premultiplied at f32 - and never in an encoded one, which hides a large error in the dark half and inflates a small one in the bright half |
| the reference | the expression evaluated at f64 where one exists, and the other implementation where it does not. A suite that compared two f32 implementations against each other alone would pass two implementations that are wrong in the same way |
| when a threshold may change | with a version change of the profile it belongs to, because the threshold is part of what conforming means |
| a freeze with no thresholds | is NOT COMPLETE, and neither is a backend measured against one. Writing these numbers is specification work and not a testing detail |
